_note: Resident-level fictional composite diagnostic-reasoning cases. This file is copied over reasoning_cases.json in the resident build. Do not include PHI. These cases teach supervised reasoning and team communication, not patient-specific diagnosis or treatment advice.

cases.title: Mania, Psychosis, Or Substance-Induced?
cases.learnerGoal: Hold competing diagnostic hypotheses, state what would update each one, and connect the formulation to safe inpatient priorities.
cases.patientBrief: A 24-year-old is admitted after four nights of little sleep, pressured speech, grand plans, irritability, religious auditory experiences, heavy cannabis use, and one recent stimulant exposure.

facts.label: Time course
facts.text: Symptoms escalated over one week; sleep decreased before the most disorganized behavior.

facts.label: Syndrome
facts.text: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, irritability, increased goal-directed activity, and poor insight.

facts.label: Substances
facts.text: Cannabis most days; one stimulant exposure. Tox data are supportive but not explanatory by themselves.

facts.label: Collateral
facts.text: Family later describes a prior week of decreased sleep, spending, and conflict that resolved without hospitalization.

steps.title: Problem Representation
steps.prompt: Which problem representation best avoids both anchoring and diagnostic sprawl?

choices.text: Young adult with acute manic syndrome, psychotic features, impaired judgment, and substance exposure, with bipolar, substance-induced, medical, and primary psychotic etiologies still being tested.
choices.feedback: Best. It names the syndrome, time course, risk, and uncertainty without converting the first impression into a final diagnosis.

choices.text: Young adult with first-episode psychosis and secondary sleep disruption, with mania to consider if psychosis persists after sobriety.
choices.feedback: This is plausible, but it reverses the chronology and underweights decreased need for sleep, increased energy, pressured speech, and grandiosity.

choices.text: Likely substance-induced psychosis or mania because cannabis and stimulant exposure are objective data while mood history is collateral.
choices.feedback: Objective data can still be misleading if interpreted without timing. Substance exposure is a contributor, not a complete formulation.

choices.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, now confirmed by collateral, with substance use addressed as a discharge issue.
choices.feedback: Collateral raises the probability of bipolar illness, but confirmation is too strong and substance use remains relevant during admission.

steps.title: Differential Discipline
steps.prompt: How should the resident present the working differential on rounds?

choices.text: Lead with manic syndrome with psychotic features; explicitly track substance-induced, medical/neurologic, and primary psychotic alternatives and the data that would move each up or down.
choices.feedback: Best. A resident-level differential is dynamic: it names the lead hypothesis and defines how uncertainty will be updated.

choices.text: Use schizoaffective disorder as the neutral diagnosis because it includes both mood and psychotic symptoms.
choices.feedback: Schizoaffective disorder is not a neutral placeholder. It requires longitudinal evidence about psychosis outside mood episodes.

choices.text: Document bipolar disorder as primary and substance-induced disorder as secondary because collateral is more reliable than tox.
choices.feedback: This may be where the formulation is heading, but the reasoning should avoid ranking evidence by source alone. Timing and recurrence matter.

choices.text: Keep the differential broad and avoid naming a leading diagnosis until several days of observation are complete.
choices.feedback: Broad uncertainty can become avoidance. The team still needs a leading syndrome and a provisional risk-informed plan today.

steps.title: Management Reasoning
steps.prompt: Which resident-level next step best links formulation to inpatient work without overreaching?

choices.text: Frame the plan around safety, sleep restoration, agitation risk, medical/substance rule-out, collateral, and supervised medication reasoning rather than a single diagnostic label.
choices.feedback: Best. It connects diagnostic reasoning to ward priorities and keeps prescribing decisions supervised and formulation-driven.

choices.text: Delay treatment planning until the substance-induced versus bipolar distinction is resolved.
choices.feedback: Inpatient care cannot wait for perfect certainty. Safety, sleep, observation, collateral, and medical workup can proceed under uncertainty.

choices.text: Prioritize antipsychotic selection because psychosis is the symptom most likely to prolong hospitalization.
choices.feedback: Medication selection may matter, but it should not eclipse sleep, mania, substances, medical contributors, safety, and alliance.

choices.text: Use the prior episode to teach the family that this is definitively bipolar disorder and substance use is not causal.
choices.feedback: This overstates certainty and can damage alliance. Psychoeducation should acknowledge probability, contributors, and what the team is still learning.

biasChecks: Do not let a positive tox screen become a complete explanation.
Do not let manic symptoms disappear behind the word psychosis.
Define what data would change your working diagnosis.

cases.title: Delirium Or New Psychosis?
cases.learnerGoal: Prioritize syndrome recognition, reversible drivers, medication risk, and consult communication when psychosis-like symptoms occur on a medical service.
cases.patientBrief: A 72-year-old post-op patient reports insects on the wall. Nursing describes waxing and waning confusion, nighttime worsening, new urinary symptoms, opioid exposure, and diphenhydramine for sleep.

facts.label: Attention
facts.text: Cannot sustain months backward; drifts off, then becomes frightened and vigilant.

facts.label: Arousal
facts.text: Somnolent in the morning, agitated after midnight, and inconsistently oriented.

facts.label: Drivers
facts.text: Post-op pain, sleep disruption, possible infection, anticholinergic exposure, and opioids.

facts.label: Baseline
facts.text: Family reports mild forgetfulness but independent function before surgery.

steps.title: Syndrome Recognition
steps.prompt: Which formulation is strongest for the consult note?

choices.text: Acute fluctuating inattention and altered arousal consistent with delirium, likely multifactorial, with visual hallucinations as part of the syndrome.
choices.feedback: Best. It makes delirium the syndrome and treats hallucinations as a feature rather than the organizing diagnosis.

choices.text: Medication-induced psychosis from anticholinergic and opioid exposure, with delirium precautions while awaiting improvement.
choices.feedback: Medication effects are plausible drivers, but the syndrome is delirium. Naming only medication-induced psychosis may narrow the workup too early.

choices.text: Dementia with behavioral disturbance precipitated by hospitalization, because family reports baseline forgetfulness.
choices.feedback: Baseline cognition affects vulnerability, but acute fluctuation and inattention should not be reduced to dementia progression.

choices.text: Late-life primary psychosis should lead because hallucinations are vivid and frightening.
choices.feedback: Late-life psychosis exists, but acute post-op fluctuation and inattention put delirium first.

steps.title: Consult Recommendation
steps.prompt: Which recommendation best balances psychiatry input with medical ownership?

choices.text: Recommend a delirium driver review, deliriogenic medication reduction where feasible, infection/metabolic/hypoxia and alcohol or sedative withdrawal assessment, sleep-wake support, mobilization, sensory aids, and supervised agitation planning.
choices.feedback: Best. It is practical, multidisciplinary, and avoids framing delirium as only a psychiatry medication problem.

choices.text: Recommend an antipsychotic only if the patient is dangerous, but otherwise defer all workup to the primary team.
choices.feedback: This respects medical ownership but is too passive. Psychiatry can help structure the reversible-driver review and nonpharmacologic plan.

choices.text: Recommend benzodiazepines for sleep if hallucinations worsen overnight, because sleep deprivation perpetuates delirium.
choices.feedback: Benzodiazepines can worsen non-withdrawal delirium. Sleep support should emphasize safer environmental and medical steps unless local supervised indications apply.

choices.text: Recommend transfer to psychiatry once medically stable because hallucinations are now the dominant symptom.
choices.feedback: The dominant syndrome is still delirium on a medical floor. Transfer framing can delay medical treatment of reversible causes.

steps.title: Family Update
steps.prompt: What is the best way to explain the reasoning to family?

choices.text: This looks like delirium: a sudden, fluctuating brain-state change often driven by medical stressors and medications; the team is looking for reversible causes while keeping the patient safe.
choices.feedback: Best. It validates the frightening symptoms, explains the syndrome, and avoids implying the patient has suddenly developed a primary psychiatric illness.

choices.text: The hallucinations are not psychiatric because they are caused by surgery and medication.
choices.feedback: The intent is reassuring, but the statement is too certain. Delirium is a neuropsychiatric syndrome with multiple contributors.

choices.text: The patient may have dementia, but we will know after the infection workup returns.
choices.feedback: Baseline cognition matters, but this explanation does not center acute delirium or the fluctuating attention problem.

choices.text: The patient is psychotic right now, so the family should avoid reinforcing the hallucinations.
choices.feedback: Do not use a primary-psychosis frame for delirium education. Family can help with reorientation, glasses/hearing aids, familiar voices, and baseline history.

biasChecks: Do not let vivid hallucinations outweigh attention and arousal.
Do not make psychiatry the owner of a medical delirium syndrome.
Name reversible drivers and what the team can do today.

cases.title: Catatonia Or Refusal?
cases.learnerGoal: Recognize catatonia while carrying dangerous mimics, medication risk, and escalation thresholds.
cases.patientBrief: A patient with severe depression is mute, staring, barely eating, and holding an awkward arm posture. Staff wonder whether the patient is refusing care or becoming psychotic again.

facts.label: Motor
facts.text: Staring, immobility, posturing, negativism, and possible waxy flexibility.

facts.label: Risk
facts.text: Poor oral intake, immobility, and concern for dehydration.

facts.label: Context
facts.text: Severe mood episode with psychotic guilt themes earlier in admission.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.text: Vitals are currently stable; medication exposure and medical contributors need review.

steps.title: Language And Differential
steps.prompt: Which chart language best supports resident-level reasoning?

choices.text: Objective motor syndrome concerning for catatonia: mutism, staring, posturing, negativism, and poor intake; assess with BFCRS and review medical, medication, delirium, and NMS/malignant features.
choices.feedback: Best. It names observed signs, uses structured assessment, and keeps dangerous mimics and complications in view.

choices.text: Psychotic depression with severe psychomotor retardation; catatonia remains possible if BFCRS is positive.
choices.feedback: This is not unreasonable, but it makes depression the organizing diagnosis before naming the motor syndrome that needs urgent assessment.

choices.text: Behavioral refusal versus catatonia; use oral intake and cooperation with nursing care to distinguish them.
choices.feedback: Catatonia cannot be separated from refusal by cooperation alone. Objective motor signs and structured assessment are needed.

choices.text: Likely malignant catatonia because poor intake is present, even though autonomic signs are absent.
choices.feedback: Malignant catatonia must be monitored for, but do not overcall it without fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, or concerning labs.

steps.title: First Move
steps.prompt: What is the safest resident next step?

choices.text: Raise catatonia urgently, obtain BFCRS, trend vitals/intake/mobility, review medications and medical drivers, and discuss supervised benzodiazepine challenge and escalation thresholds.
choices.feedback: Best. It combines recognition, measurement, medical safety, medication risk, and supervised treatment reasoning.

choices.text: Hold antipsychotic changes until BFCRS is complete, but otherwise observe because vitals are stable.
choices.feedback: Avoiding reflexive antipsychotic escalation is good, but observation alone is too passive given intake and immobility risks.

choices.text: Increase antipsychotic coverage for psychotic depression while monitoring for rigidity and fever.
choices.feedback: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia or malignant catatonia/NMS. The resident should elevate catatonia before escalating that pathway.

choices.text: Focus on capacity and refusal documentation because the patient is not eating.
choices.feedback: Capacity may become relevant, but the immediate diagnostic problem is a potentially treatable motor syndrome with medical risk.

steps.title: Escalation Threshold
steps.prompt: Which reasoning best defines when the case becomes emergent?

choices.text: Escalate urgently for fever, autonomic instability, worsening rigidity, rising CK, dehydration, immobility complications, or failure to improve with supervised first-line treatment.
choices.feedback: Best. It names the physiologic and treatment-response signals that should change urgency.

choices.text: Escalate only if the patient becomes violent or actively suicidal.
choices.feedback: Catatonia can become life-threatening through medical complications even without violence or expressed suicidality.

choices.text: Escalate if the BFCRS score is high, but vitals and oral intake are secondary.
choices.feedback: BFCRS helps quantify symptoms, but medical instability, intake, immobility, and autonomic signs drive urgency.

choices.text: Escalate when the diagnosis is certain, because premature treatment can obscure the mental status exam.
choices.feedback: Waiting for certainty can be dangerous. Catatonia is a clinical syndrome where timely supervised treatment and monitoring matter.

biasChecks: Do not treat poor cooperation as evidence against catatonia.
Do not let stable vitals erase intake and immobility risk.
Before antipsychotic escalation, ask whether catatonia or NMS is on the table.

cases.title: Crisis, Trauma, Mood, Or Personality?
cases.learnerGoal: Build a nonstigmatizing formulation that separates acute risk, trauma, mood syndrome, personality pattern, treatment targets, and team communication.
cases.patientBrief: A 28-year-old admitted after self-injury following a breakup reports chronic emptiness, childhood trauma, nightmares, mood reactivity, intermittent suicidal thoughts, and escalating conflict with staff over discharge timing.

facts.label: Risk
facts.text: Self-injury escalated after perceived abandonment; suicidal thoughts fluctuate with interpersonal stress.

facts.label: Trauma
facts.text: Nightmares, avoidance, hypervigilance, and shame themes since childhood abuse.

facts.label: Mood
facts.text: Affective shifts over hours; no sustained decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, or increased goal-directed activity.

facts.label: System
facts.text: Team members disagree: some favor rapid discharge, others feel the patient is unsafe and being rejected.

steps.title: Separate The Layers
steps.prompt: Which formulation best separates diagnosis from treatment targets?

choices.text: Acute self-harm risk after attachment rupture, with PTSD symptoms, affective instability, possible depressive disorder, and borderline personality traits; target safety, sleep, emotion regulation, alliance, and follow-up.
choices.feedback: Best. It separates acute risk, syndromes, longitudinal pattern, and immediate inpatient treatment targets without blame.

choices.text: PTSD and major depression are sufficient diagnoses for now; personality formulation can wait because it may stigmatize care.
choices.feedback: This protects against stigma, but it may miss relational risk patterns that affect alliance, discharge planning, and team consistency.

choices.text: Borderline personality disorder is the central diagnosis; trauma and depression are common comorbidities but secondary to discharge planning.
choices.feedback: This overcentralizes the label and risks flattening trauma, mood, acute safety, and collaborative treatment targets.

choices.text: Bipolar spectrum disorder should remain high because mood reactivity and impulsive self-injury can be mixed-state signs.
choices.feedback: Bipolar disorder can be missed, but the provided time course lacks sustained manic or hypomanic syndrome. Keep it as a question, not the lead.

steps.title: Team Communication
steps.prompt: How should the resident address the team disagreement?

choices.text: Name that the team may be reacting differently to the same attachment-risk cycle; align around objective risk, consistent limits, validation, discharge criteria, and one shared message.
choices.feedback: Best. It turns countertransference and team split into a structured clinical intervention.

choices.text: Ask staff to avoid reinforcing maladaptive behavior while the resident finalizes the discharge plan.
choices.feedback: Limit-setting may matter, but this wording risks blaming the patient and bypassing validation, risk formulation, and shared criteria.

choices.text: Defer discharge until the team feels comfortable, because disagreement itself means the risk is too high.
choices.feedback: Team discomfort is data, not a disposition criterion. Convert it into objective risk questions and a consistent plan.

choices.text: Avoid discussing personality dynamics with the team because it will worsen stigma.
choices.feedback: The solution to stigma is precise, compassionate formulation, not silence about dynamics that affect safety and care.

steps.title: Discharge Reasoning
steps.prompt: Which discharge formulation is most clinically useful?

choices.text: Discharge readiness depends on current suicide risk, means safety, coping plan, alliance repair, follow-up intensity, family/collateral input when appropriate, and a clear crisis plan, not diagnostic certainty alone.
choices.feedback: Best. It links formulation to actionable risk and continuity elements rather than using a diagnosis as the disposition.

choices.text: Because chronic risk is high, discharge should wait until suicidal thoughts resolve completely.
choices.feedback: Complete symptom elimination is often unrealistic. The question is whether acute risk is reduced and supports are adequate.

choices.text: Because hospitalization may reinforce dependency, discharge should proceed once the legal hold expires.
choices.feedback: This overcorrects. Avoiding iatrogenic harm matters, but legal status alone is not a clinical risk formulation.

choices.text: The safest plan is outpatient DBT referral and medication adjustment, with inpatient work focused mostly on documentation.
choices.feedback: DBT referral and medication review may help, but the inpatient resident must still address acute risk, alliance, family/collateral, and transition safety.

biasChecks: Do not let stigma decide whether you name personality patterns.
Do not let team emotion become the disposition plan.
Separate chronic baseline risk from acute modifiable risk.

cases.title: Choosing Between Augmentation Strategies
cases.learnerGoal: Confirm true treatment resistance, then choose between comparably-supported augmentation strategies using this specific patient's risk factors rather than defaulting to the option with the strongest general evidence.
cases.patientBrief: A 34-year-old woman with recurrent major depressive disorder is admitted after an intentional, since-medically-cleared overdose. She has completed an 8-week trial of sertraline 200mg with confirmed adherence and dose, and her depression has not meaningfully improved.

facts.label: Trial adequacy
facts.text: Sertraline 200mg daily for 8 weeks, adherence confirmed by pharmacy fill records and collateral; PHQ-9 22 at the start of this episode, 19 now.

facts.label: Safety context
facts.text: Admitted after an intentional overdose on an over-the-counter medication, medically cleared. Ongoing passive and intermittent active suicidal ideation.

facts.label: Medical
facts.text: Normal renal function on admission labs. No cardiac history.

facts.label: Social
facts.text: Lives alone; family is involved but works full-time and cannot provide daily supervision.

steps.title: Confirming Treatment Resistance
steps.prompt: Before calling this treatment-resistant depression, what's the resident-level move?

choices.text: Confirm the sertraline trial was adequate in dose and duration, verify adherence beyond self-report, and confirm the lack of response with a repeated standardized scale rather than clinical impression alone.
choices.feedback: Best. "Treatment-resistant" is a measurement claim before it is a diagnosis — dose, duration, adherence, and a repeated scale are what make it one.

choices.text: Move straight to discussing augmentation options with the attending, since eight weeks at a full dose is clearly enough.
choices.feedback: Eight weeks at 200mg is a reasonable adequate trial, but skipping the explicit adherence and repeated-scale check means the team is acting on impression, not confirmed data.

choices.text: Assume the lack of response reflects poor adherence outside the hospital and focus the plan on adherence counseling.
choices.feedback: Pharmacy-confirmed adherence in the fact pattern already argues against this. Defaulting to an adherence story without checking the data can delay a patient who genuinely needs a treatment change.

choices.text: Switch to a different SSRI at the same dose and reassess in another eight weeks.
choices.feedback: This restarts the clock on a patient with active suicidal ideation and a recent overdose without addressing whether escalation, not lateral switching, is what the acuity calls for.

steps.title: Choosing an Augmentation Strategy
steps.prompt: The attending asks the team to recommend an augmentation strategy. Lithium, a second-generation antipsychotic, T3, and ketamine/esketamine are all reasonable per the evidence in general. What's the best resident-level recommendation for this specific patient?

choices.text: Name that no single option is clearly superior in general, but weigh this patient's recent overdose against lithium's narrow therapeutic index and lethality in overdose, and favor an option with a wider safety margin given she will eventually be unsupervised at home.
choices.feedback: Best. Holding two comparably-supported options and still reasoning to a patient-specific answer is exactly the resident-level move — the recent overdose is data that should change the recommendation, not a detail to set aside.

choices.text: Recommend lithium first because it has the strongest anti-suicidal evidence of the options available.
choices.feedback: The anti-suicidal evidence for lithium is real, but reciting the strongest population-level evidence without weighing this patient's overdose history and eventual unsupervised access is incomplete reasoning, not a full recommendation.

choices.text: Recommend esketamine because it is the newest option and works the fastest.
choices.feedback: Speed of onset is relevant to a rapid-acting-agent discussion, but "newest" is not a reason on its own, and this skips the actual safety and access reasoning the case is asking for.

choices.text: Defer the augmentation decision entirely to the outpatient team after discharge.
choices.feedback: A patient admitted after an overdose, with a confirmed adequate-trial failure and ongoing suicidal ideation, is exactly who should not leave the hospital without a next step already started or clearly planned — deferring the whole decision abandons the acute opportunity to act.

steps.title: Integrating ECT Into The Plan
steps.prompt: Given her acute suicide risk, how should ECT be positioned in the team's recommendation?

choices.text: Raise ECT as a reasonable first-line option given the acute high suicide risk — not a last resort — and discuss it with the patient and family alongside a pharmacologic augmentation plan.
choices.feedback: Best. High acute suicide risk is one of the settings where ECT is reasonably first-line, and naming that clearly gives the patient a real choice instead of letting her default into it only after other options are exhausted.

choices.text: Mention ECT only as a distant backup if every medication option fails.
choices.feedback: This treats ECT as a last resort, which undersells how directly her acuity today — not a future failure — argues for raising it now.

choices.text: Leave ECT out of the discussion since the patient hasn't asked about it.
choices.feedback: A patient can only choose an option she's told about. Not raising a reasonably first-line option because she didn't ask isn't neutral — it's withholding it.

choices.text: Present ECT to the family as what happens when a patient hasn't tried hard enough with medication.
choices.feedback: This is both clinically inaccurate and stigmatizing. ECT's appropriateness here comes from her acuity, not from any failure on her part.

biasChecks: Do not let "strongest general evidence" substitute for patient-specific risk-benefit reasoning.
A recent overdose changes the calculus for any option with a narrow therapeutic index or overdose lethality — say so explicitly, don't just note it.
ECT is a first-line option in specific high-acuity contexts, not a failure state to mention only once other options run out.
